title: Logging Pipelines at Scale
summary: How logs travel from a running process to a searchable, affordable store, and the trade-offs that keep the bill sane.

slides.markdown:
How a log line is shaped determines whether it's queryable data or just text to grep.

| Style | Example | Queryability |
|---|---|---|
| Free-text | `User 42 checkout failed: timeout` | Only substring/regex search |
| Structured (JSON) | `{"user":42,"event":"checkout_failed","reason":"timeout"}` | Exact-field filtering, aggregation, dashboards built on log fields |

**How to decide:** structured logging costs a little more discipline at write time but pays off immediately once you have more than a handful of log lines to search — free-text logging doesn't scale past casual debugging.

Logs pass through a chain of stages, each absorbing different pressure: an **agent** on each host tails and forwards lines; a **buffer/queue** absorbs bursts; **processing** parses, filters, and enriches; **storage** holds it searchably; **query** is how it gets read back.

![The logging pipeline, source to query](assets/logging-pipeline.svg)

Each stage scales or swaps independently — "which logging tool" is really a question about five pieces.

slides.sectionTitle: Log levels and when each applies
slides.markdown:
Standard levels — `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR` — exist so volume and severity can be filtered independently of *what* is logged. `DEBUG` is local troubleshooting, usually off in prod; `INFO` marks normal but noteworthy events; `WARN` flags something recoverable; `ERROR` marks a failure needing attention.

Logging everything at `ERROR` to make sure it's seen defeats the level system — it's the ability to filter by level (drop `DEBUG` in prod, alert on `ERROR`) that levels exist to enable.

A high-traffic service can generate more log volume per second than any pipeline can affordably store — keeping *everything* isn't a real option once you're past a certain scale. **Sampling** keeps a representative fraction of routine log lines (e.g. 1-in-100 successful requests) while keeping 100% of errors and anything flagged interesting. **Filtering** drops known-noisy lines (health-check pings, verbose framework debug output) before they ever reach storage.

The goal is losing detail you'd never look at anyway, while never losing the signal you'd actually need during an incident.

Logging bills are driven by two things: **volume** (bytes ingested and stored) and, less obviously, **cardinality** in indexed fields — the same trap metrics have. Indexing a field with unbounded values (a raw request path, a user ID) as a searchable dimension can multiply index size the same way an unbounded metric label multiplies time series.

Cost control is mostly about being deliberate: sample and filter at the source (cheaper than storing then discarding), and index only the fields you'll actually query on.

slides.sectionTitle: Tracing one request with a correlation ID
slides.markdown:
Worked example: a request enters at an API gateway, which generates a **correlation ID** and passes it through every downstream call as a header. Every service logs that same ID in its structured lines. To debug one failing request, query the log store for that ID across every service, and get back an ordered picture of exactly what it did, in one search.

Without the shared ID, you'd grep each service's logs separately and guess which lines belong together — the ID turns scattered logs into one story.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: logging PII or secrets by accident
slides.markdown:
A very common, very damaging mistake: a log line includes a full request or response body "for debugging," and that payload happens to contain a password, an API key, or personal data (email, SSN, card number). Once logged, that data sits in a system that's often more widely accessible than the original request ever was, and log retention can keep it around far longer than intended.

The fix is structural: scrub or allowlist fields before logging (never log a raw request body by default), and treat "what's in this log line" as a code-review concern, not an afterthought.
